newsitem.title: GREECE: Bankers want Greece to target inflation not M3.
newsitem.headline: Bankers want Greece to target inflation not M3.

text.p: Greek monetary policy should be steered towards an inflation target rather than the current policy of targeting intermediate goals for money supply and exchange rates, some Greek bankers and economists said.
But others said intermediate money policy targets worked well and would lead to price stability, with inflation targeting an option to be exercised later when inflation was much lower.

"Inflation targeting is preferable when the link between intermediate targets and the ultimate goals of economic policy is not very stable, such as between M3 and inflation in Greece," said Fotis Siokis, a manager-economist at AT&T in New Jersey.
Financial innovations have rendered less predictable the relationship between Greek M3 and inflation and gross domestic product, said economists who pointed to an unstable M3 income velocity.

Bank of Greece uses M3 money supply and the exchange rate as intermediate policy targets with the aim of reducing anual inflation to 4.5 percent at end-97 and below 3.0 percent at end-98. It also monitors developments in M4 and total credit expansion.

But some economists said M3 targeting was secondary to the central bank's prime intermediate target of keeping the drachma stable against the major currencies that make up the ecu which explained a likely failure to hit the money supply target. "There is a trade-off between the two intermediate policy targets that makes their simultaneous attainment more difficult," said an economist at a foreign bank. "Inflation targeting offers an alternative."
Asked if inflation targeting could be combined with an exchange rate peg, the economist said the targets could be compatible provided that they were not tightly specified.
"If inflation is the prime policy goal, then putting a band around the exchange rate could ensure that targets are not inconsistent," he said.
Monetary policy has real effects on output and other economic variables in the short-run and an inflation target should be formulated so as to take these into account.

"Inflation is a monetary phenomenon but money policy has real effects in the short-run and an inflation target has to be adjusted for supply-side shocks," the economist said. "Setting an inflation range target could take care of the problem."
He added that there was need for the inflation target to be adjusted for demand-side shocks because inflation targeting produced the correct money policy response.
Other economists and bankers also said the public was better acquainted with inflation than other intermediate targets and it would be easier to hold the central bank accountable for its actions.
"Inflation targeting is also easier for the public to understand and makes the central bank more accountable for its actions," said Siokis.
But other bankers said the current setting of intermedite targets served well the goal of price stability provided that changes in M3 velocity and GDP growth were taken into account.

"To the extent that changes in M3 velocity and GDP growth are taken into account, then the use of intermediate monetary targets can lead to price stability," said Vassilis Thomas, head of sales at American Express Bank, Athens.

Other economists said they favoured a monetary policy based on inflation targeting in the future but only after price deregulation was complete and the economy found itself in a lower inflation equilibrium.

"It would be better to adhere to the hard drachma policy and other intermediate policy targets for the time being and turn to explicit inflation targeting when market price deregulation is complete and inflation is much lower," said Christofer Sardelis, chief economist at Bank of America, Athens.

Consumer price inflation firmed to 5.5 percent year-on-year in June from 5.4 percent in May but core inflation which does not include volatile food and energy prices fell to 7.0 percent from 7.6 percent in May.
A large portion of the CPI index is made up of goods and services whose prices were set administratively which limits the effectiveness of monetary policy, said Sardelis.

"Prices have to be deregulated to make CPI changes responsive to changes in monetary policy," he said. "About 60 percent of the CPI is composed of goods and services whose prices are administratevily set by the state."

Other bankers said goods and services whose prices are administratively set represented a smaller component of the CPI and pointed to mixed results on inflation despite the imposition of an essential price freeze on these goods by the government. -- Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
